CANONICAL_NAME.value: OpenSSL 1.0.1f -- the last release carrying Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)

value.lineage: OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension (RFC 6520) accepted a caller-supplied payload LENGTH and copied that many bytes back without checking it against the record actually received. 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f carry the defect; 1.0.1g fixes it with a bounds check. Preserved as the BEFORE-FAILURE body of a documented failure whose replacement is one released version away. Archival only: this fossil exists so the defect can be read in its original world, and the vault carries no exploit for it.

value.built_to: keep a TLS session alive and discover path MTU without renegotiating, per RFC 6520
value.pressure: long-lived TLS sessions over NAT/firewall timeouts needed a cheap liveness probe
value.success_means: a heartbeat reply echoing the peer's payload

value.pressure: untrusted input crossing a trust boundary into a memory-unsafe language
value.failure_condition: the responder trusted an attacker-supplied length field and echoed adjacent process memory -- disclosed as Heartbleed, fixed by bounds-checking in 1.0.1g

evidence.says: A missing bounds check in the TLS heartbeat extension allows disclosure of up to 64kB of process memory; affected versions are 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f, fixed in 1.0.1g.
The heartbeat response must echo the payload of the request; the length handling is where the implementation failed.

cut.note: the TLS/DTLS heartbeat responder (RFC 6520): it takes a request carrying a declared payload length, allocates a response sized from that declared length, and copies that many bytes from the request into the response. In 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f the declared length is used without being compared to the length of the record actually received, so a response can be larger than the request was; 1.0.1g adds two bounds checks (a zero-length guard and a check that the declared payload plus overhead does not exceed the received record) that make the responder ignore any request whose declared length is not backed by received bytes. The cut records the responder as one organ and the missing-check-then-added-check as the fossil's point

provenance.grade_basis: Techne FOSSIL_PACKET.json PROVENANCE_GRADE where issued, else the record's handoff string mapped (populated per R34; Harmonia may re-grade)

organs.human_name: tls1_process_heartbeat (t1_lib.c 2554-2611) / dtls1_process_heartbeat (d1_both.c 1455-...): read hbtype and a 16-bit payload length; on a REQUEST allocate 1 + 2 + payload + 16 and copy payload bytes then random padding, write it back; the 1.0.1g fix adds 'if (1 + 2 + 16 > s->s3->rrec.length) return 0' and 'if (1 + 2 + payload + 16 > s->s3->rrec.length) return 0' before the allocation
organs.mechanism: the responder parses a one-byte type and a two-byte declared payload length from the received record, and for a request builds a response of type, echoed length, echoed payload and 16 bytes of random padding; the read of the payload copies as many bytes as the declared length says; the defect is that nothing tied the declared length to the number of bytes actually received before 1.0.1g, so the response could be assembled from more of the process buffer than the request supplied; the fix is the two comparisons that reject a request whose declared length exceeds the received record
organs.output: a heartbeat response, or (after the fix) nothing when the declared length is unbacked
assumptions: BEFORE the fix: that a peer's declared length is backed by the bytes it sent (an untrusted-input assumption that did not hold); AFTER: the declared length must be validated against the received record
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: a keep-alive and path-MTU probe for (D)TLS without renegotiation (RFC 6520)
organs.failure_landscape: the missing bounds check is the failure: a length field consumed as a copy count without validation is the classic input-length-trust defect; the fix and CVE-2014-0160 are the recorded outcome; the DTLS copy carried the same defect, so one fossil holds two instances of the same missing check
organs.human_prior: RFC 6520 (Seggelmann et al.); the defect and fix are the CVE-2014-0160 record and the 1.0.1g changelog

pressures.source_evidence: the two handlers; the 1.0.1g bounds-check diff; RFC 6520
pressures.condition: an organism parses an untrusted message containing a length field and produces a reply built from that many bytes of an input buffer; the message's declared length may not match the bytes the peer actually sent; the score is whether the reply ever contains bytes the peer did not supply
pressures.resource_or_constraint: one comparison against the received record length
pressures.failure_condition: a reply assembled from more of the buffer than the request delivered (an over-read), which is the defect
pressures.world_punishes: trusting the declared length; sizing a copy from it without a check
pressures.world_rewards: comparing the declared length to the received length and rejecting the mismatch (the 1.0.1g fix)
pressures.observable_consequence: on a differential test between 1.0.1f and 1.0.1g with requests whose declared length exceeds the sent bytes: 1.0.1f produces an over-long response, 1.0.1g returns nothing; this is a present-vs-absent-check comparison, run in a sandboxed test harness, not an extraction against any live service
pressures.vacuity_condition: requests whose declared length always equals the bytes sent
pressures.trivial_shortcuts: rejecting all heartbeats (which the keep-alive requirement forbids)
pressures.cheat_control: the fixed release (1.0.1g) is the reference: on the same crafted-length test inputs it must never emit a response longer than the request, where 1.0.1f does; the fossil is the before, the fix is the oracle
pressures.purpose_separated_from_pressure: PURPOSE: (D)TLS heartbeat / keep-alive (RFC 6520), preserved as the CVE-2014-0160 case study
